common_name: Sordan 79 Sorghum-Sudangrass (Summer Forage & Cover Crop Hybrid)
scientific_name: Sorghum bicolor × Sorghum bicolor var. sudanense 'Sordan 79'

planting.note: Direct sow after all frost danger has passed and soil has warmed past 65°F; do not sow into cool soil.

directions: Sordan 79 is a classic sorghum-sudangrass hybrid selection long marketed for its rapid summer biomass and heat tolerance, making it a workhorse warm-season cover between spring and fall vegetable plantings. Broadcast or drill seed once soil has warmed well past the danger of frost, then mow at knee height before seed heads form to encourage denser, leafier regrowth and prevent the plant from becoming woody. Its extensive root system helps break up compacted subsoil and suppress weeds and some soilborne nematodes during the hottest months. Terminate by mowing and tilling in, or by winter-kill, several weeks before fall crops go in.

common_name: Puna II Forage Chicory (Improved Grazing & Cover Crop Chicory)

planting.note: Sow into a firm, weed-free seedbed in spring or late summer; seed is small and needs shallow, even coverage.

directions: Puna II is an improved New Zealand-bred forage chicory selected for high leaf yield, deep taproot vigor, and better persistence than older forage chicory types, and it is widely seeded into pasture and cover crop mixes for its mineral-rich, high-protein foliage. The deep taproot scavenges nutrients from well below the topsoil and helps fracture compacted ground, while the crown persists for several seasons if mowed or grazed rather than allowed to bolt and set seed. It pairs well in mixes with clovers and plantain for extended grazing or living-mulch cover in vegetable rotations. Mow periodically to prevent flowering if long-term persistence rather than reseeding is the goal.

common_name: Cosaque Winter Oat (Gulf South Forage & Cover Crop Oat)

planting.note: Drill or broadcast in early to mid-fall while soil is still warm enough for quick establishment.

directions: Cosaque is a Louisiana-developed winter oat bred specifically for reliable fall establishment and disease resistance in the humid Gulf South, where it is grown as both a grazing forage and a fast, weed-suppressing winter cover. Drill or broadcast seed in early to mid-fall so plants can build a thick canopy before the coldest weather arrives. Growth resumes rapidly in late winter, producing abundant biomass that can be grazed, cut, or simply mowed and left as mulch ahead of spring planting. Unlike cereal rye, Cosaque oat reliably winter-kills in colder zones, which can simplify spring termination without herbicide or tillage.

common_name: Laredo Forage Soybean (Indeterminate Cover Crop & Hay Soybean)

planting.note: Direct sow after soil has warmed and frost danger has passed; inoculate seed with Bradyrhizobium japonicum if soybeans are new to the bed.

directions: Laredo is a tall, leafy, indeterminate forage soybean selection bred for high dry-matter yield rather than grain, making it useful as a warm-season nitrogen-fixing cover or emergency hay crop between vegetable rotations. Its dense, vining growth quickly shades out summer weeds while root nodules add usable nitrogen for the following crop. Mow or crimp before pods fill for the best balance of biomass production and easy residue breakdown. Because it is photoperiod-insensitive, it can be sown across a wide range of latitudes without triggering premature flowering.

common_name: Maton Cereal Rye (Texas-Bred Winter Cover & Grazing Rye)

planting.note: Drill seed in fall while soil is still workable, allowing several weeks of growth before the first hard freeze.

directions: Maton is a Texas A&M-developed cereal rye selected for strong early fall growth, winter hardiness, and grazing recovery, making it popular as both a forage rye and a soil-building cover crop across the southern Plains. It tolerates close, repeated grazing or mowing better than many rye types, regrowing from the crown to provide extended winter and early-spring ground cover. Left unmowed, it produces heavy biomass and a dense root mat that suppresses weeds and scavenges residual nitrogen ahead of summer planting. Terminate by mowing, rolling, or tillage before seed set to prevent volunteer regrowth.

subcategory: winter annual cover/forage cereal grain hybrid

planting.note: Drill into a prepared fall seedbed several weeks before the first freeze so plants can tiller before dormancy.

directions: Trical 336 is a widely grown forage triticale hybrid combining rye's cold hardiness with wheat's palatability, valued for high winter biomass production and good disease resistance in cover crop and silage systems. Growth resumes vigorously in early spring, producing a tall, leafy stand that can be grazed, cut for forage, or simply mowed and left in place as a weed-suppressing mulch. Its extensive root system helps scavenge leftover soil nitrogen and improve structure ahead of summer vegetable plantings. Roll or mow at early heading for the fastest residue breakdown when used strictly as a cover.

common_name: Norcen Birdsfoot Trefoil (Cold-Hardy Pasture & Cover Legume)

planting.note: Sow shallowly into a firm seedbed in spring, using fresh or scarified seed inoculated with the correct Rhizobium strain.

directions: Norcen is a cold-hardy birdsfoot trefoil cultivar selected for improved winter survival in northern climates, grown as a long-lived perennial forage and cover legume on soils too wet, acidic, or infertile for alfalfa. Establishment is slow compared with clovers, so mow occasionally the first season to control weed competition while seedlings develop their root systems. Once established, its non-bloating foliage and deep taproot make it valuable for grazing, erosion control, and nitrogen-building cover on marginal ground for several years. It tolerates poorly drained or low-pH soils better than most other forage legumes.
